subject: ss
title: U.S. History II: Reconstruction to Civil Rights, 1865–1968
objectives: You will place the major eras of U.S. history from 1865 to 1968 in chronological order and name a defining event of each.
You will explain causes and effects of Reconstruction, industrialization, immigration, and Progressive Era reform.
You will describe U.S. involvement in the two world wars, the Great Depression and New Deal, and the Cold War policy of containment.
You will trace major achievements of the civil rights movement and the federal actions that followed.
You will answer GED-style questions using timelines, charts, and excerpts from public-domain U.S. government documents.

slides.title: U.S. History II: Reconstruction to Civil Rights
slides.board:
Week 6 Social Studies: Reconstruction to Civil Rights, 1865–1968

Today you will:

  • Put seven eras in order and name a defining event of each
  • Explain causes and effects of Reconstruction, industry, immigration, and Progressive reform
  • Describe the world wars, the Depression and New Deal, and Cold War containment
  • Trace the civil rights movement and the laws that followed
  • Answer GED questions with timelines, charts, and documents

Plan: Warm-up → seven eras → we do it together → you do it → GED questions

notes.say: Last week ended in 1865 with the Civil War and the 13th Amendment. Today we cover the next hundred years, from Reconstruction to the Voting Rights Act and the Fair Housing Act. That sounds like a lot, and it is, but the GED does not ask for hundreds of dates. It asks three things: Do you know the order of the big eras? Do you know the main cause and effect in each? Can you read a document or a chart from that time? That is exactly what we practice today.
ask: What is one event from 1865 to 1968 you already know something about? (Expected: any answer, such as World War II, the Great Depression, or Dr. King. Place it on the timeline when we reach its era.)
notes.watch: Some topics today (segregation, Japanese American incarceration, immigration limits) may connect to the student's own family. Welcome that, and keep the focus on what the documents and the record show.

slides.title: Warm-up: Week 5 Review
slides.board:
Answer each one.

  1. Put in order: Missouri Compromise; Declaration of Independence; Emancipation Proclamation; Louisiana Purchase.
  2. What did colonists mean by "no taxation without representation"?
  3. The Emancipation Proclamation (1863) freed enslaved people in which places?
  4. Which amendment, ratified in 1865, abolished slavery in the whole country?
steps: 1. Declaration of Independence (1776) → Louisiana Purchase (1803) → Missouri Compromise (1820) → Emancipation Proclamation (1863).
2. Parliament should not tax the colonists, because the colonists elected no members of Parliament. Taxes need the consent of the people's own representatives.
3. Only in the areas then in rebellion against the Union. It did not apply to loyal border states.
4. The 13th Amendment. This is where today's lesson begins.

notes.say: These four questions review last week and lead straight into today. Question 3 matters: the Emancipation Proclamation was a wartime order limited to the rebelling areas, so a constitutional amendment was needed to end slavery everywhere. Give the student about three minutes, have them say each answer, then reveal. If they miss the order in question 1, remind them to attach a year to each event first, then sort.
ask: Why was the 13th Amendment needed if the Emancipation Proclamation already existed? (Expected: the Proclamation covered only rebelling areas and was a war measure; the amendment ended slavery everywhere, permanently)
notes.answer: 1. Declaration (1776), Louisiana Purchase (1803), Missouri Compromise (1820), Emancipation Proclamation (1863). 2. Only elected representatives should be able to tax the people. 3. Areas in rebellion against the Union. 4. The 13th Amendment.
notes.watch: Students often say the Emancipation Proclamation freed all enslaved people. Correct it now, because the gap between a promise and its reach is a theme all lesson long.

notes.say: This table is the skeleton of the whole lesson. Every question this week starts with one move: put the document or event on this timeline. Notice two things. First, some eras overlap: industry kept growing during the Progressive Era, and the civil rights movement happened during the Cold War. Second, the eras connect by cause and effect. Industry created problems; Progressives tried to fix them. The Depression created a crisis; the New Deal answered it. One war ended, and a rivalry began.
ask: Which era comes between World War I and World War II? (Expected: the Great Depression and the New Deal)
Name one era that overlaps another. (Expected: industry and the Progressive Era, or the Cold War and civil rights)
notes.watch: Students often swap the order of the Depression and World War II. Anchor it: crash 1929, Roosevelt 1933, Pearl Harbor 1941.

slides.title: Worked Example: Date It, Then Order It
slides.board:
Put these in order and name the era of each:

  • The Marshall Plan
  • The Pure Food and Drug Act
  • The Freedmen's Bureau
  • The Works Progress Administration
steps: Step 1: Name the era. Freedmen's Bureau = Reconstruction. Pure Food and Drug Act = Progressive Era. Works Progress Administration = New Deal. Marshall Plan = Cold War.
Step 2: Attach a year. 1865, 1906, 1935, 1948.
Step 3: Order the eras. Reconstruction → Progressive → New Deal → Cold War.
Answer: Freedmen's Bureau → Pure Food and Drug Act → Works Progress Administration → Marshall Plan.

notes.say: Model the two-step habit out loud: era first, then year. If you know the era, you can order events even when you forget the exact year. The Freedmen's Bureau set up schools and helped formerly enslaved people. The Pure Food and Drug Act came from Progressive reporting on unsafe food. The WPA hired the jobless during the Depression. The Marshall Plan rebuilt Western Europe to keep communism from spreading.
ask: If you forgot that the WPA began in 1935, what clue would still place it? (Expected: it put jobless people to work, so it belongs to the Depression and New Deal)
notes.watch: If the student orders by "what sounds older," stop them. Every item gets an era label before anything moves.

slides.title: Reconstruction: Promise and Retreat (1865–1877)
slides.board:
Two questions in 1865: How do Southern states rejoin the Union? What will freedom mean for about 4 million formerly enslaved people?

PromiseRetreat
13th (1865): ends slavery
14th (1868): citizenship, equal protection
15th (1870): no race barrier to voting
Freedmen's Bureau; Black officeholders		Black Codes (1865–1866)
Compromise of 1877: troops leave
Jim Crow segregation laws
Poll taxes, literacy tests, violence
Plessy v. Ferguson (1896): "separate but equal"

notes.say: Reconstruction is a story of promise and retreat. The three amendments wrote freedom, citizenship, and the vote into the Constitution. The Freedmen's Bureau opened schools, and Black men voted and held office; Hiram Revels of Mississippi became the first Black U.S. senator in 1870. But Southern states passed Black Codes to control formerly enslaved workers, and Congress answered with the Reconstruction Acts of 1867, which put most of the former Confederacy under military districts. After the Compromise of 1877 removed the last federal troops, Southern states passed Jim Crow segregation laws and used poll taxes, literacy tests, and violence to keep Black citizens from voting. In 1896 the Supreme Court approved "separate but equal" in Plessy v. Ferguson.
ask: Which amendment made formerly enslaved people citizens? (Expected: the 14th)
What happened after federal troops left the South in 1877? (Expected: Jim Crow laws, segregation, and barriers to Black voting)
notes.watch: Students often think the 15th Amendment ended voting discrimination. It banned race as a reason to deny the vote, but states found other tools. Keep the phrase "law on paper vs. law in practice."

slides.title: Worked Example: Cause and Effect in Reconstruction
slides.board:
Timeline: 1865–1866: Southern states pass Black Codes.  1867: Congress passes the Reconstruction Acts.  1868: 14th Amendment ratified.

Which statement best describes the relationship between the Black Codes and the Reconstruction Acts?
steps: Step 1: Check the order. Black Codes (1865–1866) come first, so they can be a cause; the Reconstruction Acts (1867) come after, so they can be an effect.
Step 2: Ask what each did. The Black Codes limited the rights of formerly enslaved people. The Reconstruction Acts put federal military power over most Southern states.
Step 3: Connect them. Congress used federal power to protect rights the Southern states were taking away.
Answer: The Reconstruction Acts were, in part, Congress's response to the Black Codes.

notes.say: The GED loves cause-and-effect questions built on a timeline. The first test is always order: a cause must come before its effect. The second test is logic: does the later event answer or follow from the earlier one? Here it does. Congress saw Southern states rebuilding something close to slavery under a new name and took control of Reconstruction.
ask: Could the 14th Amendment (1868) be a cause of the Black Codes? Why or why not? (Expected: no, it came after them; a cause must come first)
notes.watch: "After" is not the same as "because of." Coming first is required for a cause, but it is not proof. The student also needs a logical link.

slides.title: We Do: Reconstruction Check
slides.board:
1. Which amendment do these words come from? "The right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude."
  2. Name two methods Southern states used after 1877 to keep Black citizens from voting.
  3. What did Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) allow?
steps: 1. The 15th Amendment (1870). Clue: "to vote" and "on account of race."
2. Any two: poll taxes, literacy tests, violence and intimidation (also white-only primaries and grandfather clauses).
3. State laws requiring "separate but equal" facilities, that is, legal segregation.

notes.say: Work these together. For number 1, have the student find the clue words before naming the amendment. For number 2, connect to the 15th Amendment: none of these methods mentioned race, which is how states got around it. For number 3, tell the student we will see the Supreme Court reverse course on schools in 1954.
ask: Why did poll taxes and literacy tests get around the 15th Amendment? (Expected: they did not mention race, but they were designed and enforced to block Black voters)
notes.answer: 1. 15th Amendment. 2. Poll taxes, literacy tests, intimidation (any two). 3. Legal segregation under "separate but equal."
notes.watch: Students may answer "the 14th" for number 1. Ask: "Which amendment is about voting?" The 14th is citizenship and equal protection.

slides.title: Industry, Immigration, and Progressive Reform
slides.board:
ChangeProblem it createdResponse
Railroads, steel, oil; trusts (Carnegie, Rockefeller)Monopolies crush competitionSherman Antitrust Act (1890); trust-busting
Factories, 60-hour weeksUnsafe work, child laborUnions (AFL, 1886); safety laws after Triangle fire (1911)

Muckrakers expose abusesUnsafe food, corruptionFood laws (1906); 16th–19th Amendments

notes.say: Read this table from left to right: a change, the problem it created, and the response. Industry made the United States rich and powerful, but a few trusts controlled whole industries, and factory work was long and dangerous. Workers formed unions. Immigrants came by the millions to fill factory jobs, and some Americans pushed back; the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 was the first major federal law to bar immigrants of one nationality. Then came the Progressives, about 1890 to 1920. Muckraking reporters like Jacob Riis, Ida Tarbell, and Upton Sinclair exposed problems, and government acted: the Meat Inspection Act and Pure Food and Drug Act in 1906, and four amendments: income tax (16th), direct election of senators (17th), Prohibition (18th), and women's suffrage (19th).
ask: What is a muckraker? (Expected: a Progressive Era journalist who exposed corruption or unsafe conditions)
Name the four Progressive amendments. (Expected: 16th income tax, 17th direct election of senators, 18th Prohibition, 19th women's suffrage)
notes.watch: Students mix up the Progressive Era and the New Deal because both used government to fix problems. Progressives: trusts, food, corruption, about 1890–1920. New Deal: the economic collapse of the 1930s.

slides.title: Worked Example: Read a Law
slides.board:
"Every contract, combination in the form of trust or otherwise, or conspiracy, in restraint of trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations, is hereby declared to be illegal."
(Sherman Antitrust Act, 1890, Section 1)

What did this section of the law do?
steps: Step 1: Find the subject. "Every contract, combination in the form of trust… or conspiracy."
Step 2: Find what it does. "In restraint of trade": limiting or blocking competition between businesses.
Step 3: Find the verb. "Is hereby declared to be illegal."
Answer: It made it illegal for businesses to combine into trusts or make agreements that limit competition in trade between states or with other nations.

notes.say: Laws use long, old-fashioned sentences. The trick is to strip each one down to who, does what, and what happens. Here the subject is a list of business agreements, the key phrase is "in restraint of trade," and the verb is "declared to be illegal." This was Congress's first big antitrust law. It was weakly enforced at first, but Theodore Roosevelt later used it to sue trusts, and in 1911 the Supreme Court broke up Standard Oil.
ask: Rewrite "in restraint of trade" in plain English. (Expected: holding back or limiting competition and trade)
notes.watch: Students sometimes think the law banned all big businesses. It banned combinations and agreements that restrain trade, not size alone.

By how much did immigration fall from 1921–1930 to 1931–1940, and what best explains the drop?
steps: Step 1: Compute the change. 4.1 − 0.5 = 3.6 million fewer immigrants.
Step 2: Ask what was happening then. The 1930s = the Great Depression (few jobs). Quota laws from 1921 and 1924 were also still in force.

Answer: 3.6 million fewer; the Great Depression plus the 1920s quota laws.

notes.say: A chart tells you what changed and when. It never tells you why. To explain a change, you match its dates to events you know, then check every possible explanation against those dates. Here the Depression and the quota laws both fit the 1930s. World War II does not, because the United States was not at war until the decade was over. Source: these are decade totals from the Department of Homeland Security's immigration yearbook, rounded.
ask: What event matches the drop from 8.8 million to 5.7 million in 1911–1920? (Expected: World War I made ocean travel from Europe dangerous)
notes.watch: Watch for answers that sound true but do not fit the dates, like "World War II" for the 1930s. Make the student say the years out loud.

slides.title: We Do: Progressives at Work
slides.board:
1. Upton Sinclair's novel The Jungle (1906) described filthy meatpacking plants. What laws followed that same year?
  2. A cartoon shows an octopus labeled "Standard Oil" wrapping its arms around a state capitol and the U.S. Capitol. What is the cartoonist's point?
  3. The 146 deaths in the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire (1911) led to what kind of laws?
steps: 1. The Meat Inspection Act and the Pure Food and Drug Act (both 1906).
2. One giant company (a trust) is gaining control over government itself, not just the economy.
3. Workplace safety laws (fire exits, inspections, limits on hours).

notes.say: Work these together and keep asking the same question: what problem, and what response? Number 1 is the classic muckraker chain: exposure leads to public anger, which leads to a law. In number 2, the arms show what the cartoonist fears the trust controls. Number 3 shows that tragedy also drove reform; many of the Triangle workers were young immigrant women, and locked doors kept them from escaping.
ask: In the cartoon, why does it matter that one arm reaches the U.S. Capitol? (Expected: it shows the cartoonist believes the trust is buying or controlling the national government)
notes.answer: 1. Meat Inspection Act and Pure Food and Drug Act (1906). 2. A trust is taking control of government and the economy. 3. Workplace safety laws.
notes.watch: On cartoons, students describe the picture instead of the message. Ask: "What does the cartoonist want you to believe?"

slides.title: World War I, the Depression, and the New Deal
slides.board:
World War I (U.S. 1917–1918)

  • Why the U.S. entered: German submarine attacks; Zimmermann Telegram
  • Wilson: "safe for democracy"
  • After: Senate rejects the Treaty of Versailles and the League of Nations

Depression and New Deal

  • Crash: Oct. 1929; about 25% unemployed by 1933
  • FDR's 3 Rs: Relief (help now), Recovery (restart the economy), Reform (prevent a repeat)
  • CCC, WPA, FDIC, SEC, Social Security (1935)

notes.say: World War I began in Europe in 1914. The United States stayed out until German submarines attacked ships carrying Americans, starting with the Lusitania in 1915, and until Germany's Zimmermann Telegram proposed an alliance with Mexico. Wilson asked for war on April 2, 1917; the fighting ended November 11, 1918. Afterward the Senate refused to approve the peace treaty, so the United States never joined Wilson's League of Nations. Then in October 1929 the stock market crashed; banks failed, and by 1933 about one in four workers had no job. Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal used the 3 Rs. The big lasting change: a much larger federal role in the economy and daily life.
ask: Why could the Senate block the Treaty of Versailles? (Expected: the Constitution requires two-thirds of the Senate to approve a treaty)
What is the difference between relief and reform? (Expected: relief helps people right now; reform changes the system so the crisis does not happen again)
notes.watch: Students sort every New Deal program as "relief." Ask: "Does it help people today, or does it change the rules for the future?"

slides.title: Worked Example: Relief, Recovery, or Reform?
slides.board:
The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), created in 1933, insures bank deposits so that people do not lose their savings when a bank fails.

Is the FDIC mainly relief, recovery, or reform?
steps: Step 1: Ask the relief question. Does it hand out help to people in need right now? No, it does not give out food, cash, or jobs.
Step 2: Ask the reform question. Does it change the system to prevent a future crisis? Yes: insurance protects savers in future bank failures.
Step 3: Check that it lasts. The FDIC still exists today. Permanent rule changes are the mark of reform.
Answer: reform.

notes.say: Teach the three questions in order. Relief is direct help now: jobs, food, cash. Recovery restarts business and farming. Reform changes the rules so the collapse cannot happen the same way again. Programs that still exist, like the FDIC, the SEC, and Social Security, are usually reform. Some programs did more than one job, so the GED usually asks which R a program mainly served.
ask: The Civilian Conservation Corps hired young men to plant trees and build trails. Which R? (Expected: relief, because it gave jobless people work and pay right away)
notes.watch: If the student says "recovery" for the FDIC, ask: "Does it make the economy grow now, or does it protect savers in the future?"

slides.title: World War II (U.S. 1941–1945)
slides.board:
• Road to war: Germany invades Poland (Sept. 1, 1939); U.S. sends aid through Lend-Lease (1941)
  • Entry: Japan attacks Pearl Harbor (Dec. 7, 1941); Congress declares war the next day
  • Home front: war production ends the Depression; millions of women take factory jobs
  • Incarceration: Executive Order 9066 (1942) forces about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry, most of them citizens, into camps; Congress apologizes in 1988
  • End: D-Day (June 6, 1944); Germany surrenders (May 1945); atomic bombs (Aug. 1945); Japan surrenders (Sept. 2, 1945)

notes.say: World War II began in Europe in 1939, but the United States did not fight until Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941. Roosevelt asked Congress to declare war the next day, because only Congress has that power. At home, factories ran day and night, unemployment nearly disappeared, and women took jobs once held by men. The government also violated the rights of Japanese Americans: under Executive Order 9066, about 120,000 people were forced from their homes into camps. The Supreme Court upheld it in Korematsu v. United States in 1944, and in 1988 Congress formally apologized and paid surviving victims.
ask: What ended the Great Depression, according to most historians? (Expected: massive wartime production and hiring)
Why is Japanese American incarceration a civics topic as well as a history topic? (Expected: it shows the government denying citizens their rights without due process)
notes.watch: Students confuse the two world wars. Anchors: WWI = Wilson, 1917, submarines, League of Nations. WWII = Franklin Roosevelt, Pearl Harbor, 1941, atomic bomb.

slides.title: Worked Example: A President Asks Congress
slides.board:
"I ask that the Congress declare that since the unprovoked and dastardly attack by Japan on Sunday, December 7th, 1941, a state of war has existed between the United States and the Japanese Empire."
(Franklin D. Roosevelt, Address to Congress, December 8, 1941)

What is Roosevelt asking for, and why does he ask Congress?
steps: Step 1: Date it. December 8, 1941: the day after Pearl Harbor. Era: World War II.
Step 2: Find the request verb. "I ask that the Congress declare…"
Step 3: Name the request. A declaration of war against Japan.
Step 4: Connect to civics. Article I, Section 8 gives Congress the power "To declare War." Answer: He asks Congress to declare war on Japan because only Congress has that power.

notes.say: This is a history question with a civics answer, and the GED does this constantly. The President is commander in chief, but the Constitution gives the power to declare war to Congress. Roosevelt's words show it: he does not declare war himself; he asks. Congress voted for war that same afternoon, with only one member voting no.
ask: Which earlier president in our lesson also went to Congress to ask for a declaration of war? (Expected: Woodrow Wilson, April 2, 1917)
notes.watch: Students sometimes say the Supreme Court approves wars. Ask: "Which article lists the powers of Congress?" Article I.

slides.title: The Cold War: Containment (1945–1991)
slides.board:
Cold War = U.S.–Soviet rivalry with no direct, large-scale war between the two.
Containment = U.S. policy: stop communism from spreading.

Tool of containmentExample
Money and aidTruman Doctrine (1947); Marshall Plan (1948)
AlliancesNATO (1949)
Standing firmBerlin Airlift (1948–1949); Cuban Missile Crisis (1962)
Limited warsKorea (1950–1953); Vietnam

Ends: Berlin Wall falls (1989); Soviet Union breaks apart (1991)

notes.say: After World War II the United States and the Soviet Union were the two superpowers, with opposite systems: democracy and capitalism versus communist one-party rule. They never fought each other directly on a large scale, which is why it is called a cold war, but they competed through alliances, an arms race, a space race, and wars in other countries. The American policy had one name: containment. Every tool on this table aimed to keep communism from spreading to more countries. When you see a Cold War question, ask: who acted, and did the action block the spread of communism?
ask: Why is it called the "cold" war? (Expected: the two superpowers never fought each other directly in a large-scale war)
How was the Marshall Plan a form of containment? (Expected: rebuilding Western Europe's economies made communism less attractive there)
notes.watch: Students count Soviet actions, like launching Sputnik or building the Berlin Wall, as containment. Containment is a U.S. policy, so look for U.S. actions.

slides.title: Worked Example: Is It Containment?
slides.board:
"I believe that it must be the policy of the United States to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures."
(Harry S. Truman, Address to Congress, March 12, 1947)

What policy does this sentence announce, and how does it fit the Cold War?
steps: Step 1: Date it. March 1947: two years after World War II. Era: early Cold War.
Step 2: Decode the hard word. Subjugation = being conquered or controlled. "Outside pressures" = pressure from other countries, meaning the Soviet Union.
Step 3: Name the policy. The United States will help countries resist a communist takeover. Truman asked Congress for $400 million in aid for Greece and Turkey.
Answer: The Truman Doctrine, the first big statement of containment.

notes.say: The speech never says the word "communism" in this sentence, so the student must use the date and context. In 1947 the threat Truman meant was communist pressure in Greece and Turkey, backed by the Soviet Union. This sentence became the Truman Doctrine. A year later, the Marshall Plan applied the same idea to all of Western Europe with economic aid.
ask: What clue tells you this is about the Cold War and not World War II? (Expected: the date, 1947, after World War II ended)
notes.watch: Students may say the speech is about going to war. Truman asked for money and advisers, not a declaration of war.

slides.title: We Do: Containment or Not?
slides.board:
For each event, say whether it is a U.S. act of containment.

  1. The United States, Canada, and ten European nations form NATO (1949).
  2. The Soviet Union launches Sputnik, the first artificial satellite (1957).
  3. U.S. troops, under the United Nations, defend South Korea after North Korea invades (1950).
  4. East Germany builds the Berlin Wall (1961).
steps: 1. Yes. A U.S.-led military alliance to defend Western Europe against Soviet expansion.
2. No. A Soviet action. It sparked the space race, but it was not a U.S. policy.
3. Yes. U.S. forces fought to stop communist North Korea from taking over the South.
4. No. East Germany, a Soviet ally, built it to stop people from fleeing to the West.

notes.say: Use one test for each item: who acted, and did the action block communism from spreading? This exact skill shows up as a select-two or select-three question on the GED, and the wrong answers are almost always real Cold War events carried out by the other side.
ask: What was the U.S. response to the Berlin Wall? (Expected: it did not tear it down; it protested and kept supporting West Berlin. The Wall fell in 1989.)
notes.answer: 1. Yes. 2. No (Soviet action). 3. Yes. 4. No (East German action).
notes.watch: If the student says yes to Sputnik because "it is part of the Cold War," point out the difference between a Cold War event and a U.S. containment action.

slides.title: The Civil Rights Movement (1948–1968)
slides.board:
Who actedWhat happened
PresidentExecutive Order 9981 (1948): equal treatment in the armed forces
Supreme CourtBrown v. Board of Education (1954): school segregation unconstitutional
CitizensMontgomery Bus Boycott (1955–1956); Greensboro sit-ins (1960); March on Washington (1963); Selma marches (1965)
CongressCivil Rights Act (1964); 24th Amendment (1964); Voting Rights Act (1965); Fair Housing Act (1968)

notes.say: Black Americans and their allies attacked segregation from every direction: in court, on buses, at lunch counters, and in the streets. In 1954 the Supreme Court ruled in Brown that "separate educational facilities are inherently unequal," reversing the idea behind Plessy for schools. Rosa Parks's arrest in December 1955 began a bus boycott that lasted more than a year. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. led nonviolent protest and civil disobedience, and at the 1963 March on Washington he described his hope for a nation where people would be judged by their character, not their color. Congress then acted: the Civil Rights Act of 1964 outlawed segregation in public places and job discrimination; the Voting Rights Act of 1965 attacked literacy tests and other barriers; the Fair Housing Act of 1968 banned discrimination in housing.
ask: Which branch acted in Brown, and which acted in the Civil Rights Act? (Expected: the Supreme Court; Congress)
What is civil disobedience? (Expected: peacefully and openly breaking a law you believe is unjust and accepting the penalty)
notes.watch: Do not hand out texts of Dr. King's speeches or letters; they are not in the public domain. Describe them. On the GED, expect excerpts from laws, court opinions, and presidential speeches.

slides.title: Worked Example: Compare Two Federal Actions
slides.board:
A: "…there shall be equality of treatment and opportunity for all persons in the armed services without regard to race, color, religion or national origin." (Executive Order 9981, President Truman, 1948)

B: No voting rule "shall be imposed or applied by any State or political subdivision to deny or abridge the right of any citizen of the United States to vote on account of race or color." (Voting Rights Act, Congress, 1965)

How are they alike and different?
steps: Step 1: Alike. Both use federal power against racial discrimination.
Step 2: Who acted? A is an executive order from the President. B is a law passed by Congress.
Step 3: What area? A covers the armed forces. B covers voting rules made by states and local governments.
Answer: Both fight discrimination, but A is a presidential order about the military and B is an act of Congress about voting.

notes.say: For any two-document question, compare on three lines: who wrote it, when, and what it covers. Read the source lines before the excerpts; they answer the first two. Point out a detail the GED likes to test: Excerpt A lists race, color, religion, and national origin, while Excerpt B lists only race or color. Switching those lists is a classic trap answer.
ask: Why could Truman act alone on the armed forces? (Expected: the President is commander in chief of the military)
notes.watch: Students sometimes call an executive order a law passed by Congress. Ask: "Who signed it, and did Congress vote?"

Have the student do the subtraction and say the units: percentage points. Source: U.S. Commission on Civil Rights. Then ask what the data can and cannot prove: it shows a rise after the law, and the law's tools explain why, but the table alone does not prove the law was the only cause.
ask: Which state had the larger increase? (Expected: Mississippi, 53.1 points; Alabama rose 32.3 points)
notes.answer: 1. 53.1 percentage points. 2. Literacy tests, poll taxes, and intimidation kept Black citizens from registering. 3. The Voting Rights Act of 1965.
notes.watch: Students may write "53.1%" or try a percent change. When you subtract two percentages, the answer is in percentage points.

slides.title: You Do 1: Reconstruction to the Progressive Era
slides.board:
On your own (3 minutes).

  1. Which amendment guaranteed "equal protection of the laws"?
  2. What event in 1877 ended Reconstruction?
  3. Name the book that exposed the meatpacking industry in 1906.
  4. Which amendment, ratified in 1920, gave women the right to vote?
steps: 1. 14th Amendment. 2. The Compromise of 1877 (federal troops withdrawn from the South). 3. The Jungle, by Upton Sinclair. 4. The 19th Amendment.

notes.say: Now the student works alone. Start a three-minute timer and stay quiet. When time is up, have the student give all four answers before you reveal. If they miss one, send them to that era's screen in the Student Lesson.
ask: For number 2, what happened in the South after the troops left? (Expected: Jim Crow laws and voting barriers)
notes.watch: If the student says "15th" for number 1, remind them: 14th = citizenship and equal protection; 15th = voting and race.

slides.title: You Do 2: Wars, Depression, and Cold War
slides.board:
On your own (3 minutes).

  1. What event brought the United States into World War II?
  2. Social Security (1935) gives pensions to retired workers. Which R of the New Deal is it mainly?
  3. Name the U.S. Cold War policy of stopping the spread of communism.
  4. True or false: The Senate approved the Treaty of Versailles, and the United States joined the League of Nations.
steps: 1. Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor (Dec. 7, 1941). 2. Reform (a permanent system of protection). 3. Containment. 4. False: the Senate rejected the treaty, so the U.S. never joined the League.

notes.say: Same routine: three minutes, quiet, then the student reports. For number 2, require the reason, not just the label. For number 4, ask what part of the Constitution made the Senate's vote decisive.
ask: For number 4, how many senators must approve a treaty? (Expected: two-thirds of the senators present)
notes.watch: If the student calls Social Security relief, ask whether it helps only during the crisis or protects people permanently.

slides.title: You Do 3: Civil Rights and Data
slides.board:
On your own (3 minutes).

  1. Which 1954 Supreme Court case ruled segregated public schools unconstitutional?
  2. Alabama Black voter registration: 19.3% (1965) → 51.6% (1967). Change in percentage points?
  3. Executive order or act of Congress: the Civil Rights Act of 1964?
  4. Fact or opinion: "The Montgomery Bus Boycott lasted more than a year."
steps: 1. Brown v. Board of Education. 2. 51.6 − 19.3 = 32.3 percentage points. 3. Act of Congress. 4. Fact: it can be checked in records (December 1955 to December 1956).

notes.say: Last solo round. Three minutes, then the student reports. On number 2, require the units. On number 4, ask how they know: a fact can be checked; an opinion is a judgment people can disagree with.
ask: How would you change number 4 into an opinion? (Expected: add a judgment, such as "The boycott was the most important protest in American history.")
notes.answer: 1. Brown v. Board of Education. 2. 32.3 percentage points. 3. Act of Congress. 4. Fact.
notes.watch: If the student answers 32.3% or computes a percent change for number 2, review: subtract two percentages to get percentage points.

slides.title: GED Question 1: A Presidential Address
slides.board:
"The world must be made safe for democracy…. We have no selfish ends to serve. We desire no conquest, no dominion. We seek no indemnities for ourselves…." (Woodrow Wilson, Address to Congress, April 2, 1917)

Why did Wilson most likely include these statements?

A. To warn Germany that the U.S. planned to take German territory
B. To assure Americans the U.S. would fight for principles, not for land or wealth
C. To announce that the U.S. would remain neutral in the war
D. To ask Congress to make Germany pay the costs of the war
steps: Eliminate A. It reverses the text. "We desire no conquest" means no taking of territory.
Eliminate C. Wilson was asking Congress for a declaration of war; this is the opposite of neutrality.
Eliminate D. Indemnities are payments for damages, and Wilson says "We seek no indemnities."
Answer B. "No selfish ends," "no conquest," and "safe for democracy" present the war as a fight for principles.

notes.say: Have the student choose before you reveal, then walk through each elimination with its reason. Two wrong answers here are reversals of the text, and one ignores the context (the date tells you this is the war message). Point out how much the source line helped: April 1917 means Wilson is asking for war.
ask: What does "dominion" mean here? (Expected: control or rule over other lands or peoples)
notes.answer: B. To assure Americans the United States would fight for principles, not for land or wealth.
notes.watch: Students who pick D may not know "indemnities." Teach the habit: when a hard word decides the answer, find its meaning from context or the glossary line.

slides.title: GED Question 2: Data and Causes
slides.board:
Immigrants admitted (millions): 1901–1910: 8.8  |  1911–1920: 5.7

Which event best explains the decrease from 1901–1910 to 1911–1920?

A. World War I made ocean travel from Europe dangerous and difficult.
B. The Great Depression left few jobs for newcomers.
C. The Chinese Exclusion Act stopped immigration from Europe.
D. The Cold War closed the borders of Eastern Europe.
steps: Eliminate B. The Depression began in 1929, after this decade ended. Wrong dates.
Eliminate C. The Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) applied to Chinese laborers, not Europeans, and it came decades earlier.
Eliminate D. The Cold War began after 1945. Wrong dates.
Answer A. World War I (1914–1918) falls inside 1911–1920 and disrupted Atlantic crossings from Europe, where most immigrants then came from.

notes.say: This is the "date check" strategy in action. Three of the four answers are real events that did reduce immigration at some point, which is why they are tempting. Only one happened during the decade in the question. Have the student say each event's dates out loud before eliminating it.
ask: Which answer would explain the drop in 1931–1940 instead? (Expected: the Great Depression)
notes.answer: A. World War I made ocean travel from Europe dangerous and difficult.
notes.watch: Students who choose B are matching "big event that lowered immigration" without checking dates. Make them write the years next to each option.

slides.title: GED Strategy: Date the Document First
slides.board:
1. Read the source line first: who wrote it, and when?
  2. Place the date on the Big Timeline: which era, which president, which problem?
  3. Read the question, then the excerpt or chart.
  4. Date-check every answer. An effect cannot come before its cause.
  5. Charts show what, not why. Bring in a dated event or a document to explain a change.

Pace: about 2 minutes per question on the Social Studies test.

notes.say: History questions on the GED almost always come with a source line. That line is free information. Knowing a document is from April 1917 or December 1941 tells you which war, which president, and which problems the country faced, and it often rules out two answers before you read closely. Practice this habit on every question this week: before reading the excerpt, say the era out loud.
ask: A speech is dated March 1933. What era, and what problem? (Expected: the Great Depression; Franklin Roosevelt just took office)
notes.watch: Strong readers skip the source line and dive into the text. Make them stop and say the date and era every time until it is automatic.

screens.title: What You Will Learn
screens.html:
About one fifth of the GED Social Studies test is U.S. history, and much of it comes from the hundred years after the Civil War. You will read short pieces of laws, court rulings, and presidential speeches, study charts and timelines, and decide what caused an event or what it led to. You do not need to memorize hundreds of dates. You do need the order of the big eras and the main idea of each.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • Put the major eras from 1865 to 1968 in order and name a defining event of each
  • Explain causes and effects of Reconstruction, industrialization, immigration, and Progressive reform
  • Describe the two world wars, the Great Depression and New Deal, and the Cold War policy of containment
  • Trace the civil rights movement and the federal actions that followed
  • Answer GED-style questions using timelines, charts, and government documents

Each screen teaches one idea and ends with a quick check. Answer it before you move on.

screens.title: The Big Timeline
screens.html:
Here is the map for the whole lesson. Learn the order of these seven eras first; every other fact hangs on it.

EraYearsAnchor event
Reconstruction1865–187713th, 14th, 15th Amendments
Industry and immigrationabout 1865–1900Transcontinental railroad (1869)
Progressive Eraabout 1890–1920Food safety laws (1906)
World War IU.S. at war 1917–1918U.S. declares war (April 1917)
Depression and New Deal1929–1941Stock market crash (1929)
World War IIU.S. at war 1941–1945Pearl Harbor (December 7, 1941)
Cold War and civil rights1945–1968 and beyondBrown v. Board (1954); Voting Rights Act (1965)

Some eras overlap. Industry kept growing during the Progressive Era, and the civil rights movement took place during the Cold War.

example.prompt: Put in order: NATO is formed; Reconstruction ends; the New Deal begins; Progressive food safety laws pass.
steps: Name each era and year: Reconstruction ends (1877); food safety laws, Progressive Era (1906); New Deal begins (1933); NATO, Cold War (1949).
Order the eras: Reconstruction, Progressive, New Deal, Cold War.
example.answer: Reconstruction ends → food safety laws → New Deal begins → NATO is formed.

check.prompt: Drag each event into its place in time, from earliest (1st) to latest (4th).
choices: The stock market crashes and the Great Depression begins.
The 15th Amendment bans denying the vote because of race.
Japan attacks Pearl Harbor.
Upton Sinclair’s The Jungle leads to new food safety laws.
check.why: The most common mistake is placing the stock market crash after Pearl Harbor. The Depression began in 1929, and the United States did not enter World War II until 1941.
check.hint: Name the era of each event first, then use the Big Timeline.
check.explain: Attach an era and a year to each event: 15th Amendment (1870, Reconstruction); The Jungle and food safety laws (1906, Progressive Era); stock market crash (1929, Depression); Pearl Harbor (1941, World War II). The order is 15th Amendment, The Jungle, the crash, Pearl Harbor.

screens.title: Reconstruction: Three Amendments
screens.html:
When the Civil War ended in 1865, the nation faced two big questions: how to bring the Southern states back into the Union, and what freedom would mean for about four million formerly enslaved people. The period from 1865 to 1877 is called Reconstruction.

13th Amendment (1865): abolished slavery.
14th Amendment (1868): made everyone born in the United States a citizen and promised "the equal protection of the laws."
15th Amendment (1870): banned denying the vote "on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude."

Congress also created the Freedmen's Bureau (1865), which set up schools and helped formerly enslaved people find work and family members. Black men voted and won office; Hiram Revels of Mississippi became the first Black U.S. senator in 1870.

A memory trick: 13 = free, 14 = citizen, 15 = vote.

check.prompt: Which amendment made formerly enslaved people citizens and promised all persons "the equal protection of the laws"? Type the number only.

mistakes.why: The 15th Amendment is about voting. Citizenship and equal protection come from the amendment just before it.
The 13th Amendment ended slavery. It did not define citizenship; the next amendment did.

check.hint: Use the trick: 13 = free, 14 = citizen, 15 = vote.
check.explain: The 14th Amendment (1868) says all persons born or naturalized in the United States are citizens and forbids any state to "deny to any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws." Use the trick: 13 = free, 14 = citizen, 15 = vote.

screens.title: The End of Reconstruction and Jim Crow
screens.html:
Many white Southerners resisted these changes. In 1865 and 1866, Southern states passed Black Codes that limited where formerly enslaved people could work and travel. Congress answered with the Reconstruction Acts of 1867, which put most of the former Confederacy under military districts.

Reconstruction ended with the Compromise of 1877, which led to the withdrawal of the last federal troops from the South. Then Southern states passed Jim Crow laws that segregated Black and white Americans in schools, trains, and public places. They kept Black citizens from voting with poll taxes (a fee to vote), literacy tests, and violence. None of these rules mentioned race, which is how states got around the 15th Amendment.

In Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), the Supreme Court allowed segregation as long as facilities were "separate but equal." In practice, they were rarely equal.

check.prompt: Which development most directly followed the withdrawal of federal troops from the South in 1877?
options: Southern states passed Jim Crow segregation laws and set up barriers to Black voting.
Congress passed the 13th Amendment to abolish slavery throughout the nation.
The Supreme Court ruled in Brown v. Board that segregated schools were unconstitutional.
Congress created the Freedmen’s Bureau to build schools for formerly enslaved people.
why: The 13th Amendment was ratified in 1865, twelve years before the troops left. An effect must come after its cause.
Brown v. Board came in 1954, and it moved in the opposite direction, striking down school segregation.
The Freedmen’s Bureau was created in 1865, during Reconstruction, not after it ended.
check.hint: An effect has to come after its cause. Check the year of each choice.
check.explain: Once federal troops left in 1877, no federal force protected Black citizens' rights in the South. Southern states passed Jim Crow laws and used poll taxes, literacy tests, and violence to block Black voters. The 13th Amendment and the Freedmen's Bureau both date from 1865, before the troops left, and Brown came in 1954.

screens.title: Industry, Trusts, and Unions
screens.html:
After the Civil War, the United States became an industrial giant. The transcontinental railroad was finished on May 10, 1869, linking the coasts into one national market. Andrew Carnegie built a steel empire, and John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil came to control most of the nation's oil refining.

Companies that combined to control a whole industry were called trusts or monopolies. With no competition, they could set prices and crush small businesses. Congress passed the Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) to outlaw combinations "in restraint of trade."

Factory workers often worked 60 hours a week in dangerous conditions for low pay, and children worked in mills and mines. Workers formed labor unions, such as the American Federation of Labor (1886), to bargain together for better wages, hours, and safety.

check.prompt: Why did factory workers in the late 1800s join labor unions?
options: To bargain together with employers for better pay, shorter hours, and safer conditions
To help large companies combine into trusts that could control entire industries
To persuade Congress to stop all immigration so that wages for factory jobs would stay high
To run for office in Congress and replace the business owners who served there
why: This reverses the roles. Trusts were combinations of companies; unions were organizations of workers.
Some workers did oppose immigration, but that was not the purpose of a union. Unions existed to bargain with employers.
Unions did not exist to run candidates for Congress. Their main tool was bargaining together with employers.
check.hint: What can workers do as a group that one worker cannot do alone?
check.explain: A labor union is an organization of workers who bargain together with employers. One worker asking for a raise could be fired; a whole union asking was much harder to ignore. Trusts, by contrast, were combinations of companies.

screens.title: Immigration and Backlash
screens.html:
Factories needed workers, and millions of immigrants came to fill those jobs. Before 1890 most came from northern and western Europe; after 1890, more came from southern and eastern Europe, such as Italy, Poland, and Russia. Ellis Island in New York Harbor opened as an immigration station in 1892. Most immigrants settled in fast-growing cities and took factory jobs.

Some Americans pushed back. The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 was the first major federal law to bar immigrants of one nationality. In the 1920s, quota laws (1921 and 1924) sharply limited immigration from southern and eastern Europe and barred most immigration from Asia.

example.prompt: The Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) said that "the coming of Chinese laborers to the United States be, and the same is hereby, suspended." What did the law do?
steps: Find the subject: "the coming of Chinese laborers."
Find what happens to it: "suspended," which means stopped for a time.
example.answer: It stopped Chinese workers from immigrating to the United States. (The ban was set for ten years; later laws extended it until 1943.)

check.prompt: As used in the Chinese Exclusion Act, the word suspended most nearly means
options: stopped for a period of time
welcomed with special treatment
taxed at a higher rate
moved to a different port
why: This reverses the meaning. The act was meant to keep Chinese laborers out, not welcome them.
The excerpt says nothing about taxes. A suspension stops something; it does not charge for it.
Nothing in the excerpt mentions ports. Suspended means paused or stopped, not relocated.
check.hint: Think of a student who is "suspended" from school.
check.explain: To suspend something is to stop it for a time. The law stopped "the coming of Chinese laborers" for ten years, and later laws kept the ban in place until 1943. The law's title, the Chinese Exclusion Act, also tells you it kept people out.

screens.title: Immigration in Numbers
screens.html:
GED charts often track immigration. This table shows how many immigrants were admitted in each decade, in millions.

DecadeImmigrants (millions)
1881–18905.2
1891–19003.7
1901–19108.8
1911–19205.7

Source: U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Yearbook of Immigration Statistics (decade totals, rounded).

Charts show what changed, not why. To explain a change, match its dates to events you know. The 1911–1920 drop overlaps World War I. The 1920s decline follows the quota laws. The collapse in the 1930s matches the Great Depression.

example.prompt: How many more immigrants, in millions, arrived in 1901–1910 than in 1891–1900?
steps: Read both rows: 1901–1910 = 8.8; 1891–1900 = 3.7.
Subtract: 8.8 − 3.7 = 5.1.

check.prompt: Using the table, by how many million did immigration fall from 1911–1920 to 1921–1930?

mistakes.why: You used 1931–1940 (4.1 − 0.5). The question compares 1911–1920 with 1921–1930: 5.7 − 4.1.
You added the two values. A fall is a difference, so subtract: 5.7 − 4.1.

check.hint: Find the two rows named in the question and subtract.

screens.title: The Progressive Era
screens.html:
The Progressive Era (about 1890–1920) was a response to the problems of industry and city growth. Progressives believed government should protect ordinary people from big business, unsafe conditions, and corruption.

Reporters called muckrakers exposed abuses. Jacob Riis photographed crowded city tenements (1890). Ida Tarbell investigated Standard Oil (1902–1904). Upton Sinclair's novel The Jungle (1906) described filthy meatpacking plants, and that same year Congress passed the Meat Inspection Act and the Pure Food and Drug Act. After the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire killed 146 workers in 1911, New York passed new safety laws.

Four amendments came out of this era:

AmendmentYearWhat it did
16th1913Federal income tax
17th1913Voters elect U.S. senators directly
18th1919Prohibition of alcohol
19th1920Women's right to vote

check.prompt:
Complete the statement.

Journalists who exposed unsafe food and corruption were called {{0}}. Upton Sinclair's The Jungle helped lead to the {{1}} in 1906, and the 19th Amendment (1920) {{2}}.

options: muckrakers
trusts
unions
suffragists
why: Trusts were the giant companies that Progressive journalists often attacked, not the journalists.
Unions were organizations of workers. The journalists who exposed abuses had a different name.
Suffragists campaigned for women’s right to vote. The question asks about reporters who exposed abuses.

options: Meat Inspection Act
Chinese Exclusion Act
Sherman Antitrust Act
Social Security Act
why: The Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) restricted immigration. The Jungle was about meatpacking.
The Sherman Act (1890) targeted trusts and came 16 years before The Jungle.
Social Security (1935) was a New Deal program, nearly 30 years later.

options: gave women the right to vote
created a federal income tax
banned the sale of alcohol
let voters elect senators directly
why: The income tax is the 16th Amendment.
Prohibition is the 18th Amendment.
Direct election of senators is the 17th Amendment.

check.hint: Use the amendment table on this screen for the last blank.
check.explain: Muckrakers were the reporters who exposed abuses. The Jungle described meatpacking plants and led to the Meat Inspection Act (and the Pure Food and Drug Act) in 1906. The 19th Amendment gave women the right to vote. The 16th, 17th, and 18th Amendments covered the income tax, the direct election of senators, and Prohibition.

screens.title: World War I
screens.html:
World War I began in Europe in 1914. At first the United States stayed neutral. Then German submarines attacked ships carrying Americans, including the British liner Lusitania in 1915, and in 1917 Germany announced it would sink any ship near Britain. Germany also sent the Zimmermann Telegram, which proposed an alliance with Mexico against the United States.

On April 2, 1917, President Woodrow Wilson asked Congress to declare war, saying "the world must be made safe for democracy." Congress declared war four days later. The fighting ended with an armistice on November 11, 1918.

After the war, Wilson wanted the United States to join a League of Nations. But a treaty needs the approval of two-thirds of the Senate, and the Senate rejected the Treaty of Versailles. The United States never joined the League.

check.prompt: Why did the United States never join the League of Nations?
options: The Senate did not approve the Treaty of Versailles, which included the League.
President Wilson refused to sign the treaty that created the League.
The Supreme Court ruled that the League violated the Constitution.
Germany and Mexico formed an alliance that blocked American membership in the League.
why: This reverses Wilson’s role. The League was Wilson’s own idea, and he pushed hard for it.
The Supreme Court did not rule on the League. Treaties are approved by the Senate, not by the courts.
The Zimmermann Telegram only proposed a German-Mexican alliance during the war. It had nothing to do with the League afterward.
check.hint: Which branch must approve a treaty?
check.explain: The Constitution requires two-thirds of the Senate to approve a treaty. The Senate rejected the Treaty of Versailles, so the United States never joined the League of Nations, even though the League was President Wilson's idea. This is a history fact with a civics reason: checks and balances on the treaty power.

screens.title: The Great Depression and the New Deal
screens.html:
In October 1929 the stock market crashed. Banks failed, factories closed, and by 1933 about one in four workers had no job. In the Great Plains, drought and dust storms (the Dust Bowl) drove many farm families west.

President Franklin D. Roosevelt took office in March 1933. His New Deal aimed at the "3 Rs":

Relief: help for the jobless and hungry right now (Civilian Conservation Corps, Works Progress Administration)
Recovery: get business and farming working again (public works, farm programs)
Reform: change the system so a collapse would not happen again (FDIC, Securities and Exchange Commission, Social Security)

The big change: the federal government took a much larger role in the economy and in people's daily lives.

example.prompt: The FDIC insures bank deposits so people do not lose their savings when a bank fails. Relief, recovery, or reform?
steps: Does it hand out help right now? No. Does it restart business? Not directly.
Does it change the system to prevent a future crisis? Yes: it protects savers in future bank failures.

check.prompt: Drag each New Deal program into the goal it mainly served.
choices: The Civilian Conservation Corps gives jobless young men paid work planting trees and building trails.
The Securities and Exchange Commission sets rules for the stock market to prevent another crash.
The Social Security Act creates a permanent system of old-age pensions.
The Works Progress Administration hires millions of unemployed people to build roads and schools.
check.why: The most common mistake is putting Social Security under relief because it gives people money. It created a permanent system to protect future retirees, which makes it reform.
check.hint: Ask: does it help people right now, or does it change the rules for the future?
check.explain:
• Relief: the CCC and the WPA put jobless people to work and gave them paychecks right away.
  • Reform: the SEC and Social Security changed the system permanently: stock market rules to prevent another crash, and pensions to protect people in old age.

screens.title: World War II
screens.html:
World War II began in Europe when Germany invaded Poland on September 1, 1939. The United States sent weapons and supplies to Britain through Lend-Lease (1941) but stayed out of the fighting until Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on December 7, 1941. The next day, President Roosevelt asked Congress to declare war on Japan, because only Congress has that power.

On the home front, war factories ended the Depression, and millions of women took jobs once held by men. The government also violated the rights of Japanese Americans. Under Executive Order 9066 (1942), about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry on the West Coast, most of them U.S. citizens, were forced into incarceration camps. In 1988 Congress formally apologized and paid surviving victims.

The Allies landed in France on D-Day (June 6, 1944). Germany surrendered in May 1945. After atomic bombs struck Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August, Japan formally surrendered on September 2, 1945.

check.prompt: Which statement about the home front during World War II is accurate?
options: War production created so many jobs that unemployment fell and the Depression ended.
Most factories closed because so many workers had joined the armed forces.
Japanese Americans were exempt from wartime rules because most were U.S. citizens.
Women were barred by federal law from working in factories that made weapons.
why: This reverses what happened. Factories expanded and ran around the clock to supply the war.
Citizenship did not protect them. About 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry, most of them citizens, were forced into camps.
No such law existed. Millions of women took factory jobs, including in weapons plants.
check.hint: Think about what happened to jobs when the country needed ships, planes, and tanks.
check.explain: War production created millions of jobs, and unemployment fell to very low levels, ending the Great Depression. Factories expanded rather than closed, women took millions of industrial jobs, and Japanese Americans, most of them citizens, were incarcerated under Executive Order 9066.

screens.title: The Cold War and Containment
screens.html:
After World War II, the United States and the Soviet Union became rival superpowers. They never fought each other directly on a large scale, which is why it is called a "cold" war. They competed through alliances, an arms race, a space race, and wars in other countries.

The U.S. policy was containment: keep communism from spreading to more countries.

  • Truman Doctrine (1947): aid to Greece and Turkey to resist communist pressure
  • Marshall Plan (1948): aid to rebuild Western Europe
  • Berlin Airlift (1948–1949): food and fuel flown into West Berlin during a Soviet blockade
  • NATO (1949): a military alliance to defend Western Europe
  • Korean War (1950–1953) and the Vietnam War: wars to stop communist expansion in Asia

The Cuban Missile Crisis (1962) was the closest the two sides came to nuclear war. The Cold War ended when the Berlin Wall fell (1989) and the Soviet Union broke apart (1991).

check.prompt: Which actions were part of the U.S. policy of containment? Select two answers.
options: The Marshall Plan sends aid to rebuild Western Europe.
The Soviet Union launches the satellite Sputnik.
The United States joins NATO to defend Western Europe.
The Soviet Union breaks apart into 15 countries.
why: This was a Soviet action. Containment was a U.S. policy, so look for things the United States did.
The breakup of the Soviet Union ended the Cold War. It happened inside the Soviet Union and was not a U.S. containment action.
check.hint: Containment was a U.S. policy. Who carried out each action?
check.explain: The Marshall Plan made Western Europe stronger and less open to communism, and NATO promised to defend it. Both were U.S. actions to stop communism from spreading. Sputnik was a Soviet launch, and the Soviet breakup in 1991 ended the Cold War.

screens.title: The Civil Rights Movement
screens.html:
Black Americans and their allies challenged segregation in courts, on buses, at lunch counters, and in the streets.

  • 1948: President Truman's Executive Order 9981 called for equal treatment in the armed forces.
  • 1954: In Brown v. Board of Education, the Supreme Court ruled that "separate educational facilities are inherently unequal," ending legal school segregation.
  • 1955–1956: Rosa Parks's arrest in Montgomery, Alabama, sparked a bus boycott that lasted more than a year.
  • 1960: Students began sit-ins at whites-only lunch counters in Greensboro, North Carolina.
  • 1963: At the March on Washington, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. spoke of his hope for a nation where people would be judged by their character, not their skin color.
  • 1965: Marches from Selma to Montgomery, Alabama, demanded voting rights.

Dr. King and many others used civil disobedience: peacefully and openly breaking a law they believed was unjust, and accepting the penalty.

check.prompt: Click the sentence that states an opinion rather than a fact.
spans: On February 1, 1960, four Black college students sat down at a whites-only lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina.
They were refused service but stayed in their seats until the store closed.
Within weeks, sit-ins had spread to other cities across the South.
The students showed more courage than any other protesters of their time.
In July 1960, the Greensboro lunch counter began serving Black customers.
check.why: The most tempting wrong click is the sentence about sit-ins spreading. "Within weeks" sounds like a judgment, but it is a time fact that records can confirm.
check.hint: A fact can be checked in records. Look for a judgment word like "most," "best," or "more than any other."
check.explain: "The students showed more courage than any other protesters of their time" is a judgment that people could reasonably disagree with, and no record can prove it. That makes it an opinion. Every other sentence states a date, an action, or an outcome that can be checked in records.

screens.title: The Laws That Followed
screens.html:
The movement pushed all three branches of the federal government to act.

Federal actionBranchWhat it did
Executive Order 9981 (1948)PresidentEqual treatment in the armed forces
Brown v. Board (1954)Supreme CourtEnded legal school segregation
Civil Rights Act (1964)CongressBanned segregation in public places and job discrimination
24th Amendment (1964)Congress and the statesBanned poll taxes in federal elections
Voting Rights Act (1965)CongressAttacked literacy tests and sent federal examiners to register voters
Fair Housing Act (1968)CongressBanned discrimination in selling and renting housing

Notice the gap: the 15th Amendment banned race-based denial of the vote in 1870, yet the Voting Rights Act was needed in 1965. A right on paper is not always a right in practice.

example.prompt: How are Executive Order 9981 and the Voting Rights Act alike, and how are they different?
steps: Alike: both use federal power against racial discrimination.
Different: the order came from the President and covered the armed forces; the act was passed by Congress and covered voting.
example.answer: Both fight discrimination, but one is a presidential order about the military and the other is a law of Congress about voting.

check.prompt: Why was the Voting Rights Act of 1965 needed, even though the 15th Amendment had banned race-based denial of the vote in 1870?
options: Some states used literacy tests, poll taxes, and threats to block Black voters.
The 15th Amendment had been repealed by Congress during the Great Depression.
The 15th Amendment applied only to elections for president, not to state elections.
Women did not yet have the right to vote, so the 15th Amendment had no effect.
why: The 15th Amendment was never repealed. It was still in the Constitution in 1965; the problem was enforcement.
The 15th Amendment covers denial of the vote "by the United States or by any State," not only presidential elections.
Women won the vote in 1920 through the 19th Amendment, decades before 1965. That is not why the 1965 act was needed.
check.hint: Think about the gap between a law on paper and how it was enforced.
check.explain: The 15th Amendment was the law on paper, but some states got around it with literacy tests, poll taxes, and intimidation, none of which mentioned race. The Voting Rights Act gave the federal government tools to stop those practices. The amendment was never repealed, it covers state as well as federal elections, and women had been voting since 1920.

screens.title: Reading Historical Documents: Date It First
screens.html:
Most GED history questions give you a document with a source line: who wrote it and when. Read that line before anything else.

1. Who wrote it, and when?
2. Place the date on the Big Timeline: which era, which president, which problem?
3. Read the question, then the excerpt.
4. Check every answer against the date. An effect cannot come before its cause.

Example: "So, first of all, let me assert my firm belief that the only thing we have to fear is fear itself." The source line says Franklin D. Roosevelt, First Inaugural Address, March 4, 1933. That date puts you in the worst year of the Great Depression, when banks were failing and one in four workers had no job. Now the meaning is clear: Roosevelt is trying to calm a frightened nation.

check.prompt: A speech is dated March 12, 1947. A student says the speech is probably about how to end the Great Depression. Why is that unlikely?
options: By 1947 World War II was over, and the main foreign-policy issue was the rivalry with the Soviet Union.
In 1947 the Great Depression had not yet begun, so the speaker could not discuss it.
In 1947 the United States had just entered World War I, so leaders talked only about the fighting in Europe.
By 1947 the civil rights movement had ended, and the speaker would have discussed its results.
why: The Depression began in 1929, so by 1947 it was long past, not yet to come.
The United States entered World War I in 1917, thirty years earlier.
The civil rights movement was just beginning in 1947; Brown and the Voting Rights Act came later.
check.hint: Place 1947 on the Big Timeline. Which era had just ended, and which had begun?
check.explain: The Depression ended during World War II (1941–1945). In 1947 the country had entered the early Cold War, and that is exactly when President Truman gave the speech that became the Truman Doctrine. Dating the document rules out the Depression, World War I, and the end of the civil rights movement.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
• Reconstruction (1865–1877): 13th (free), 14th (citizen, equal protection), 15th (vote). After the Compromise of 1877: Jim Crow, poll taxes, literacy tests; Plessy (1896).
  • Industry and immigration: railroads, trusts, unions; Chinese Exclusion Act (1882); quota laws (1921, 1924).
  • Progressive Era (about 1890–1920): muckrakers; food laws (1906); 16th–19th Amendments.
  • World War I (1917–1918): submarines, Zimmermann Telegram; Senate rejects the League of Nations.
  • Depression and New Deal: crash (1929); relief, recovery, reform; bigger federal role.
  • World War II (1941–1945): Pearl Harbor; war jobs end the Depression; Japanese American incarceration.
  • Cold War: containment through aid, alliances, and limited wars.
  • Civil rights: EO 9981 (1948), Brown (1954), Civil Rights Act (1964), Voting Rights Act (1965), Fair Housing Act (1968).
  • Skills: date the document first; charts show what changed, not why; subtract percentages to get percentage points.

Next: the Practice set. Read every explanation, even on questions you get right.

items.prompt: According to the timeline, which event happened before Congress passed the Reconstruction Acts?
options: Southern state governments passed Black Codes.
The 14th Amendment was ratified.
Hiram Revels became the first Black U.S. senator.
The last federal troops were withdrawn from the South.
why: The 14th Amendment was ratified in 1868, one year after the Reconstruction Acts of 1867. It is close in time, so check the year carefully.
Revels became a senator in 1870, three years after the Reconstruction Acts.
The troops left in 1877, which is ten years after the Reconstruction Acts and marks the end of Reconstruction.
items.hint: Find the year of the Reconstruction Acts, then look at the rows above it.
items.explain:
The Reconstruction Acts were passed in 1867. The Black Codes were passed in 1865–1866, which is earlier.

The 14th Amendment (1868), Hiram Revels's election (1870), and the withdrawal of troops (1877) all came after 1867. A common mistake is choosing the 14th Amendment because it is close in time; check the year: 1868 comes after 1867.

items.skill: Main idea of a primary source
items.prompt: What was the main purpose of the section of the law shown in Document 1?
options: To stop Chinese laborers from coming to the United States for ten years
To allow Chinese laborers to become U.S. citizens after ninety days
To require every immigrant arriving in the United States to pass a written test
To end all trade between the United States and the Chinese Empire
why: The "ninety days" is only the waiting period before the ban began. The law says nothing about citizenship.
The law names only "Chinese laborers," not all immigrants, and it mentions no test.
The law is about laborers coming to live and work, not about trade. Trade is never mentioned.
items.hint: Find the word that tells what happens to "the coming of Chinese laborers."
items.explain:
The law says that "the coming of Chinese laborers to the United States be, and the same is hereby, suspended" from ninety days after passage "until the expiration of ten years." To suspend means to stop for a time. So the law stopped Chinese workers from immigrating for ten years.

The "ninety days" is only the waiting period before the ban began; the law says nothing about citizenship. It applies only to Chinese laborers, not to all immigrants, and it says nothing about trade.

items.prompt: According to the chart, how many more immigrants, in millions, were admitted in 1901–1910 than in 1931–1940?

mistakes.why: You used the 1921–1930 bar (8.8 − 4.1). The question asks about 1931–1940, which is 0.5 million.
You added the two bars. "How many more" means find the difference: 8.8 − 0.5.
You used the 1941–1950 bar (8.8 − 1.0). The question asks about 1931–1940, the lowest bar.

items.hint: Read both bars, then subtract the smaller value from the larger one.
items.explain:
1901–1910: 8.8 million

Difference: 8.8 − 0.5 = 8.3 million
