items.prompt: Which development best explains the low number of immigrants shown for 1931–1940?
options: The Great Depression left few jobs, and 1920s quota laws still limited entry.
The opening of Ellis Island in New York Harbor made it harder for immigrants to enter.
The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 ended immigration from Europe for the decade.
The United States fought in World War II all decade, so ships could not cross the ocean.
why: Ellis Island opened in 1892 to process immigrants, and immigration was very high in the decades after it opened.
The Chinese Exclusion Act applied to Chinese laborers, not to Europeans, and it came fifty years earlier.
Check the dates: the United States did not enter World War II until December 1941, after this decade ended.
items.hint: What was happening to the U.S. economy in the 1930s? What laws about immigration had already been passed?
items.explain:
In the 1930s the Great Depression caused massive unemployment, so there were few jobs to attract immigrants, and the quota laws of 1921 and 1924 were still in force. Together they explain the drop from 4.1 million to 0.5 million.

Ellis Island opened in 1892 as an immigration station, and immigration was very high in the decades after it opened. The Chinese Exclusion Act applied to Chinese laborers, not Europeans. The United States did not enter World War II until December 1941, after this decade ended.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the cartoonist's point of view?
options: One powerful company is taking control of small business, transportation, and government.
Large oil companies help small grocery stores and railroads by keeping prices low.
State governments have grown more powerful than the national government in Washington.
Newspapers are spreading false and unfair stories about the American oil industry.
why: Nothing in the cartoon shows the trust helping anyone. The grocer "looks on helplessly" while an arm squeezes his store.
The cartoon shows the trust grabbing both capitols. It does not compare state and federal power.
The newspaper asks a question, "WHO RULES?" It is not shown spreading falsehoods, and the cartoon is critical of the trust, not the press.
items.hint: Look at what each arm of the octopus is grabbing, and at the headline the public is reading.
items.explain:
The octopus is labeled "THE OIL TRUST," and its arms squeeze a grocery store (small business), a railroad car (transportation), and a state capitol, while reaching for the U.S. Capitol (government). The headline "WHO RULES?" asks whether the trust, not the people, controls the country. The cartoonist sees the trust as a dangerous monopoly, a typical Progressive Era view.

Nothing in the cartoon suggests the trust helps anyone; the grocer looks helpless. The cartoon does not compare state and federal power, and the newspaper is shown as asking a question, not spreading falsehoods.

items.prompt: Drag each event into the era in which it took place.
choices: Upton Sinclair’s The Jungle leads Congress to pass the Meat Inspection Act.
The Civilian Conservation Corps hires young men to plant trees and build trails.
The Berlin Airlift flies food and fuel into West Berlin.
Ida Tarbell publishes an investigation of Standard Oil.
President Roosevelt signs the Social Security Act.
The United States and Western European nations form NATO.
items.why: The most common mistake is putting Social Security in the Progressive Era because it is a reform. Check the date (1935) and the president (Franklin D. Roosevelt): it belongs to the New Deal.
items.hint: Progressive Era: about 1890–1920. New Deal: the 1930s. Cold War: after 1945.
items.explain:
• Progressive Era: The Jungle and the Meat Inspection Act (1906); Ida Tarbell's Standard Oil investigation (published 1902–1904). Both are muckraker actions against big business.
  • New Deal: the Civilian Conservation Corps (1933) and the Social Security Act (1935). Both are Roosevelt programs responding to the Great Depression.
  • Cold War: the Berlin Airlift (1948–1949) and NATO (1949). Both were efforts to contain Soviet power.

A common mix-up is putting Social Security in the Progressive Era because it is a reform; check the date (1935) and the president (Franklin D. Roosevelt).

items.prompt: Why did President Wilson most likely include the statement "We desire no conquest, no dominion" in his address?
options: To assure Americans that the nation would fight for principles, not land or power
To warn Germany that the United States planned to take over German territory
To explain to Congress that the United States would remain neutral in the war
To ask Congress to pay for the war with money taken from Germany afterward
why: This reverses the text. "No conquest" means the United States does not want to take territory.
Wilson was asking Congress to declare war, the opposite of staying neutral. The background note says Congress declared war four days later.
"We seek no indemnities" means Wilson is not asking for payments from Germany.
items.hint: Conquest means taking land by force; dominion means control over others. What is Wilson saying the United States does NOT want?
items.explain:
Wilson says the United States has "no selfish ends," wants "no conquest, no dominion," and seeks "no indemnities" (payments). He is presenting the war as a fight to make the world "safe for democracy," not a grab for territory or wealth. That reassures Americans that the cause is just.

He says the opposite of wanting German territory. He is asking for war, not neutrality. And "We seek no indemnities" means he is not asking for payments from Germany.

items.prompt:
Complete the statement based on Document 3.

Roosevelt says the Social Security Act will help people through unemployment compensation and {{0}}. He admits that the law {{1}}. The act is best described as part of the New Deal goal of {{2}}.

options: old-age pensions
free college tuition
guaranteed farm prices
government jobs for every citizen
why: College tuition is never mentioned. The benefits listed are unemployment compensation, old-age pensions, and services for children and health.
Farm prices were handled by other New Deal programs. This statement does not mention farms.
The act gives "some measure of protection," not jobs for everyone. Work programs like the WPA were separate.

options: cannot protect every person against every hardship
will end all poverty within ten years
covers one hundred percent of the population
replaces all state welfare programs
why: Roosevelt makes no such promise. He says the law gives only "some measure of protection."
This reverses his words. "We can never insure one hundred percent of the population" means the law does not cover everyone.
Nothing in the statement mentions state welfare programs.

options: reform, creating a lasting system of protection against future hardship
winning World War II
breaking up monopolies
limiting immigration
why: The act was signed in 1935, six years before the United States entered World War II.
Breaking up monopolies was a Progressive Era goal (the Sherman Act and trust-busting), not the purpose of Social Security.
Social Security has nothing to do with immigration. It protects workers against job loss and poverty in old age.

items.hint: Reread the list of benefits in the first paragraph and the sentence that begins "We can never insure."
items.explain:
Blank 1: The first paragraph lists "unemployment compensation," "old-age pensions," and services for children and health. Old-age pensions is correct.

Blank 2: "We can never insure one hundred percent of the population against one hundred percent of the hazards" means the law cannot protect every person against every hardship. The choice "covers one hundred percent of the population" reverses his meaning.

Blank 3: Social Security created a permanent program to protect people against job loss and poverty in old age in the future. That is reform. Breaking up monopolies was a Progressive Era goal, and the act came six years before the United States entered World War II.

items.prompt: In Document 4, Roosevelt asks Congress, rather than acting alone, to declare that a state of war exists. Which constitutional principle explains why?
options: The Constitution gives Congress the power to declare war.
The Constitution gives the Supreme Court the power to approve wars.
The Constitution requires the states to vote before a war begins.
The Constitution lets the President declare war only in election years.
why: The Supreme Court decides cases; it has no role in approving wars. Article I gives the war power to Congress.
The states do not vote on declarations of war. That power belongs to Congress under Article I.
No rule ties the war power to election years. The President never has the power to declare war alone.
items.hint: Think back to Week 2: which branch has the power to declare war under Article I?
items.explain:
Article I, Section 8 of the Constitution lists the powers of Congress, including the power "To declare War." The President is commander in chief of the armed forces, but only Congress can formally declare war. That is why Roosevelt says, "I ask that the Congress declare…" Congress voted for war on Japan the same day, December 8, 1941.

The Supreme Court does not approve wars, the states do not vote on declarations of war, and no rule ties the war power to election years.

items.prompt: The U.S. Cold War policy of containment aimed to stop the spread of communism. Which events in the timeline are examples of the United States carrying out containment? Select three answers.
options: Aid to Greece and Turkey (1947)
Formation of NATO (1949)
U.S. troops defend South Korea (1950)
Launch of Sputnik (1957)
Building of the Berlin Wall (1961)
Breakup of the Soviet Union (1991)
why: Sputnik was launched by the Soviet Union. It is a Cold War event, but not a U.S. action to contain communism.

The Soviet breakup ended the Cold War. It happened inside the Soviet Union and was not itself a U.S. action.
items.hint: Look for actions the United States itself took to block communist expansion. Who carried out each of the other events?
items.explain:
• Aid to Greece and Turkey (1947): the Truman Doctrine helped those nations resist communist pressure.
  • NATO (1949): a military alliance to defend Western Europe against Soviet expansion.
  • Defending South Korea (1950): U.S. troops fought to stop communist North Korea from taking over the South.

Sputnik was launched by the Soviet Union, and the Berlin Wall was built by East Germany; neither was a U.S. action. The breakup of the Soviet Union ended the Cold War; it happened inside the Soviet Union and was not itself a U.S. containment action.

items.prompt: Read the account of the civil rights movement below. Click the sentence that states an opinion rather than a fact.
spans: On December 1, 1955, Rosa Parks was arrested in Montgomery, Alabama, for refusing to give up her bus seat to a white passenger.

The boycott was the most important protest in the history of the United States.

Within a decade, Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
items.why: The most tempting wrong click is the sentence about the Supreme Court ruling, because "unconstitutional" sounds like a judgment. It is a fact: the Court did issue that ruling in 1956, and records confirm it.
items.hint: A fact can be checked in records. An opinion is a judgment that people could reasonably disagree with. Look for words like "best" or "most important."
items.explain:
"The boycott was the most important protest in the history of the United States" is a judgment. Historians could argue for other protests, and no record can prove it. That makes it an opinion.

Every other sentence can be checked: the date and place of Parks's arrest, the length of the boycott, the 1956 Supreme Court ruling, King's role as a leader, and the dates of the 1964 and 1965 laws.

Check the source lines. Excerpt A is an executive order from the President, and Excerpt B is an act of Congress. Neither is a court ruling or an amendment.
items.hint: Check the source line under each excerpt: who issued it, and what area of life does it cover?

Excerpt A is Executive Order 9981, issued by President Truman, and it covers "all persons in the armed services." Excerpt B is Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, a law passed by Congress, and it covers "the right…to vote." So they differ in both who acted and what area they cover, even though both target discrimination.

The choice about religion reverses the documents: Excerpt A lists "race, color, religion or national origin," while Excerpt B lists only "race or color." Excerpt B is the one aimed at "any State or political subdivision." Neither excerpt is a court ruling or an amendment.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the table?
options: Unemployment fell after 1933 but stayed above 14 percent in each New Deal year shown.
The New Deal had brought unemployment all the way back down to its 1929 level by 1937.
Unemployment rose every year shown, from 1929 through the end of World War II.
World War II pushed unemployment to the highest level shown anywhere in the table.
why: In 1937 unemployment was still 14.3 percent, more than four times the 1929 level of 3.2 percent.
Unemployment fell after 1933 and dropped to 1.2 percent by 1944. It did not rise every year.
This reverses the data. The highest rate is 24.9 percent in 1933; during the war it fell to 4.7 and then 1.2 percent.
items.hint: Compare 1929 with 1937, and find the first year the rate fell below 5 percent.
items.explain:
Unemployment fell from 24.9 percent (1933) to 14.3 percent (1937), then rose again to 19.0 percent (1938). It dropped below 5 percent only in 1942, after the United States entered World War II (4.7 percent), and reached 1.2 percent in 1944. So the New Deal years brought improvement, but the rate stayed above 14 percent in every New Deal year shown; the steep drop came with wartime production.

The most tempting wrong answer says the New Deal restored the 1929 level by 1937, but 14.3 percent is far above 3.2 percent.

mistakes.why: That is the change in percentage points (24.9 − 14.3). For percent change, divide that change by the starting value: 10.6 ÷ 24.9.

items.hint: Find the change first, then divide by the 1933 value.
items.explain:
Step 1: change = 24.9 − 14.3 = 10.6 percentage points.
Step 2: divide by the starting value: 10.6 ÷ 24.9 ≈ 0.4257.
Step 3: 0.4257 ≈ 43 percent.

The most tempting wrong answer is 10.6, which is the change in percentage points, not the percent decrease.

items.prompt: Which pair of events from the timeline shows an event followed by its most direct effect?
options: Federal troops leave the South (1877) → Southern states pass Jim Crow laws (1880s–1890s)
Southern states pass Jim Crow laws (1880s–1890s) → Federal troops leave the South (1877)
The Freedmen’s Bureau is created (1865) → Plessy v. Ferguson upholds segregation (1896)
The 15th Amendment is ratified (1870) → The 13th Amendment abolishes slavery (1865)
why: This reverses the order. The troops left in 1877, before the Jim Crow laws, so the laws cannot have caused the withdrawal.
The order is right, but there is no direct link. The Bureau helped formerly enslaved people; Plessy came 31 years later from a challenge to a Louisiana railroad law.
An effect cannot come before its cause. The 13th Amendment (1865) came five years before the 15th (1870).
items.hint: Check two things for each pair: does the first event come first, and did it actually lead to the second?
items.explain:
Once the last federal troops left in 1877, no federal force protected Black citizens' rights in the South. In the following years, Southern states passed Jim Crow segregation laws and adopted poll taxes and literacy tests. The withdrawal came first and made the laws possible, so it is a cause followed by its effect.

Two choices fail the order test (an effect cannot come before its cause). The Freedmen's Bureau and Plessy are in the right order, but one did not lead to the other, which is the trap: coming first is necessary for a cause, but it is not enough.

items.prompt: What was the main purpose of Section 1 of the Sherman Antitrust Act?
options: To make business combinations that limit trade or competition illegal
To require every large company to register with the federal government
To protect the right of workers to form labor unions and go on strike
To set the prices that railroads and oil companies could charge customers
why: Section 1 says nothing about registering companies. It declares certain combinations "illegal."
Labor unions are not mentioned. The law targets combinations "in restraint of trade," meaning business deals that block competition.
The law does not set any prices. It outlaws combinations and monopolies that restrain trade.
items.hint: Strip the sentence down: what kinds of agreements, and what does the law declare them to be?
items.explain:
Section 1 says that "every contract, combination in the form of trust or otherwise, or conspiracy, in restraint of trade" is "hereby declared to be illegal." Restraint of trade means limiting or blocking competition. So the law made business combinations that limit competition illegal.

The law does not mention registering companies, labor unions, or prices. A common misreading is that it set prices for big companies; it only outlawed combinations that restrain trade.

items.prompt: Which development best explains the trend shown in the chart?
options: Factory jobs drew rural Americans and new immigrants to growing cities.

New Deal work programs hired millions of jobless people in the cities.

The quota laws of 1921 and 1924 limited immigration, and they came after the chart’s last year, 1920.
The New Deal began in 1933, more than a decade after the chart ends.

items.explain:
From 1870 to 1920 the United States industrialized. Factories, mills, and railroads were based in cities, and the jobs drew people from farms and millions of immigrants. That explains the steady rise from 25.7 percent to 51.2 percent; by 1920, for the first time, more than half of Americans lived in urban areas.

The Dust Bowl and the New Deal belong to the 1930s, and the quota laws reduced immigration starting in 1921, so none of them fits the dates on the chart.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the cartoonist's point of view?

Trusts were a Progressive Era target. This cartoon is about Roosevelt’s New Deal agencies, shown by their letters.

items.prompt: Drag each event into the era in which it took place.

Millions of women take jobs building ships and airplanes for the war effort.

Congress passes the Voting Rights Act after the Selma marches.

items.hint: Reconstruction: 1865–1877. World War II: 1941–1945 for the United States. Civil rights movement: mostly the 1950s and 1960s.
items.explain:
• Reconstruction: Hiram Revels becomes a senator (1870); the Freedmen's Bureau opens schools (1865 and after).

items.prompt: Why did President Roosevelt most likely say "the only thing we have to fear is fear itself"?
options: To calm a frightened public and build confidence that the nation could recover
To warn Americans that a foreign enemy was preparing to attack the country
To announce that the Depression was already over and no new action was needed
To blame ordinary Americans for causing the bank failures by acting in fear
why: In March 1933 the crisis was economic, not military. Pearl Harbor was more than eight years away.
Roosevelt says the nation "will revive," which means it has not recovered yet, and he calls for action: "put people to work."
He calls the fear "unjustified" and says it "paralyzes needed efforts," but he does not blame the public for the bank failures.
items.hint: Read the background note first. What was the mood of the country on March 4, 1933?
items.explain:
The background says thousands of banks had failed and one in four workers had no job. Roosevelt says the nation "will endure," "will revive and will prosper," and that fear "paralyzes needed efforts to convert retreat into advance." His purpose is to calm the public and build confidence so that recovery can begin.

The date rules out a foreign attack, and "will revive" shows the Depression was not over. The tempting trap is reading "unjustified terror" as blaming the public; he is describing fear as the obstacle, not accusing people of causing the crisis.

isolationism
the New Deal

The New Deal was Roosevelt’s response to the Depression at home, not a foreign policy.
Trust-busting was a Progressive Era policy against monopolies, not a Cold War policy.

the President is not allowed to discuss foreign affairs
the Supreme Court must approve all aid to other nations
each state must vote before the nation sends aid abroad
why: The President leads foreign policy and is giving this very speech about it. The issue is money, which Congress controls.
The Supreme Court decides cases; it does not approve foreign aid.
States do not vote on foreign aid. Congress, which controls federal spending, decides.

items.hint: Find the sentence that begins "I believe that our help should be primarily…" and the last sentence of the excerpt.

items.prompt: More senators voted for the Treaty of Versailles than against it. Why did the treaty still fail?
options: A treaty needs two-thirds of the senators present, and 49 of 84 is less than that.
A treaty also needs a majority vote of the House, and the House did not vote on it.
A treaty needs the approval of the Supreme Court, which ruled against the League.
A treaty needs a majority of all 96 senators, and only 35 senators voted against it.
why: The excerpt gives the treaty power to the President and the Senate only. The House does not vote on treaties.
The Supreme Court has no role in approving treaties. The Constitution gives that job to the Senate.
Forty-nine is already more than half of 96, so a simple majority would have passed it. The rule is two-thirds of senators present.
items.hint: Add the votes, then find two-thirds of that total.
items.explain:
Article II requires that "two thirds of the Senators present concur." In March 1920, 49 + 35 = 84 senators voted. Two-thirds of 84 is 56. Only 49 voted yes, so the treaty fell short by 7 votes, even though the yes votes outnumbered the no votes.

The House does not vote on treaties, and the Supreme Court does not approve them. The tempting trap is thinking a majority is enough; for treaties, the Constitution requires two-thirds.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes how Excerpt A and Excerpt B are related?

Check the background notes. Excerpt A is from Plessy (1896, railroad cars), and Excerpt B is from Brown (1954, schools).
Both excerpts are Supreme Court opinions, not laws or amendments. Read the source line.
items.hint: Read the background note above each excerpt. Who wrote Excerpt A, and did that justice agree with the Court?
items.explain:
Harlan says "Our Constitution is color-blind" and "neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens," so he rejects separating people by race. Brown says "Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal." Both reject legal separation by race. But Harlan wrote a dissent; the Court ruled against his view in 1896. In Brown, the opinion was the Court's unanimous ruling, and it became the law.

The most tempting wrong answer says Excerpt A supports "separate but equal." That is true of the Plessy majority, but Excerpt A is the dissent.

The Voting Rights Act was the only cause of the rise in registration in these five states.

An effect cannot come before its cause. Executive Order 9981 (1948) came six years before Brown (1954).

items.prompt: Southern states passed Black Codes in 1865 and 1866. Which part of the 14th Amendment most directly challenged those laws?
options: No state may deny any person the equal protection of the laws.
Citizens may vote in federal elections without paying a poll tax.
Congress may collect taxes on incomes from whatever source derived.
The right to vote may not be denied on account of a person’s sex.
why: Banning poll taxes in federal elections is the 24th Amendment (1964), not the 14th. It is not in the excerpt.
The income tax is the 16th Amendment (1913), a Progressive Era change unrelated to the Black Codes.
Voting regardless of sex is the 19th Amendment (1920). The Black Codes targeted formerly enslaved people, not women.
items.explain: The Black Codes were state laws that limited the rights of formerly enslaved people. Section 1 of the 14th Amendment made them citizens and forbade any state to "deny to any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws." The other choices describe the 24th, 16th, and 19th Amendments, none of which appear in the excerpt.

items.prompt: In 1911 a fire at the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory in New York City killed 146 workers, many of whom were trapped behind locked doors. What was one effect of this event?
options: New York passed laws requiring fire exits, inspections, and safer working conditions.
Congress passed the Chinese Exclusion Act to limit the number of factory workers.
Congress passed the Sherman Antitrust Act to break up the clothing industry trust.
President Roosevelt created the Works Progress Administration to rebuild the factory.
why: The Chinese Exclusion Act was passed in 1882, almost thirty years before the fire. An effect must come after its cause.
The Sherman Act was passed in 1890, before the fire, and it targeted monopolies, not workplace safety.
The WPA was a New Deal program created in 1935. It had nothing to do with this fire.
items.explain: The fire showed how dangerous factories were, and public anger led New York to pass new workplace safety laws: fire exits, sprinklers, inspections, and limits on hours. This is a classic Progressive Era chain: a problem is exposed, and government responds. The Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) and the Sherman Act (1890) came earlier, and the WPA (1935) came much later.

  • Recovery (restart the economy): public works, farm programs
